issues.claim: the CNIL sets no threshold but expects a published justification
issues.source_says: The CNIL confirms it sets no threshold ('Il n'appartient pas a la CNIL de fixer un seuil') but only encourages publication: 'Pour plus de transparence a l'egard des internautes, la CNIL encourage les editeurs a publier leur analyse.' Encouragement, not an expectation.

issues.claim: It applies to any publisher serving French users.
issues.source_says: The page frames the criteria as first criteria to be applied case by case ('ils doivent etre utilises dans le cadre d'une analyse au cas par cas'), not as a rule of general application.

proposed_takeaway: The CNIL sets out when conditioning access on consent can still yield free consent: a real and equitable alternative must exist, a paid alternative must be reasonably priced (the CNIL sets no threshold but encourages publishers to publish their pricing analysis), consent must be requested only for trackers needed to monetise the free path, and the paid path may carry only strictly necessary trackers, with separate consent for third-party content. The criteria are applied case by case to publishers serving French users. Document the pricing rationale and audit the paid path for stray advertising or analytics tags.
note: Substance is right; only the strength of the publication expectation is overstated.

issues.claim: The Conseil d'Etat upheld the decision on 28 January 2022.
issues.source_says: The deliberation of 7 December 2020 predates any appeal; it only notes that a recours may be brought before the Conseil d'Etat within four months. The 28 January 2022 judgment (no. 449209) is outside this document.

issues.claim: fined Google LLC 60 million euros and Google Ireland Limited 40 million euros
issues.source_says: The published text of SAN-2020-012 is anonymised (societe X, societe Y, [...].fr) because the two-year naming period has expired; the amounts 60 000 000 and 40 000 000 euros under article 82 are in the dispositif, and SAN-2021-023 at paragraph 7 attributes 60 million to GOOGLE LLC and 40 million to GOOGLE IRELAND LIMITED.

issues.claim: around 40 advertising cookies were written to French users' terminals on arrival
issues.source_says: Point 87: 'quel que soit le parcours de l'utilisateur ... plus de 40 cookies poursuivant une finalite publicitaire etaient deposes' (more than 40, not around 40).

issues.claim: The Conseil d'Etat confirmed the sanction on 27 June 2022 (decision no. 451423).
issues.source_says: The 7 December 2020 deliberation predates any appeal and says nothing about later judicial review.

proposed_takeaway: The CNIL found that more than 40 advertising cookies were written to French users' terminals on arrival at amazon.fr, whether from the home page or from third-party advertisements, and that the banner text (offer and improve our services) described neither the advertising purpose nor the means of refusal, in breach of article 82. The fine was 35 million euros with a three-month injunction backed by 100,000 euros per day. Landing pages reached from advertising links need the same banner as the home page. The Conseil d'Etat confirmed the sanction on 27 June 2022 (decision no. 451423).
note: Banner wording, 35 million euro fine, three-month injunction and 100,000 euro daily astreinte all confirmed in the operative part.

issues.claim: a 100 million euro fine
issues.source_says: The decision reviews two fines totalling 100 million euros: 60 million on Google LLC and 40 million on Google Ireland Limited.

note: One-stop-shop held inapplicable to article 82 enforcement, market share above 90 percent, about 47 million French users and the refusal of a preliminary reference to the CJEU are all in the decision.

issues.claim: The decision is the CNIL's clearest statement that a first-layer reject-all button is mandatory.
issues.source_says: Paragraphs 125 to 129 and the dispositif require a refusal mechanism of equivalent simplicity to acceptance; the first-layer 'Tout refuser' button is only 'fortement preconise' in the recommendation of 17 September 2020, which the formation restreinte says merely clarifies the statutory duty. The decision does not mandate a particular button.

issues.claim: The CNIL later closed the injunction after Google added a reject all button.
issues.source_says: Not addressed; the closure was decided separately by deliberation SAN-2023-012 of 13 July 2023.

proposed_takeaway: The CNIL fined Google LLC 90 million euros and Google Ireland Limited 60 million euros because google.fr and youtube.com offered a one-click accept button but required several clicks to refuse all cookies, which the CNIL held discourages refusal and invalidates consent under article 82. An injunction required a refusal mechanism as simple as acceptance within three months, backed by 100,000 euros per day of delay. The decision is the CNIL's clearest statement that refusing must be as simple as accepting, which in practice means a reject all control on the first layer. The CNIL later closed the injunction after Google added a reject all button.
note: Dispositif confirms 90 million on GOOGLE LLC, 60 million on GOOGLE IRELAND LIMITED, article 82, three months, 100,000 euros per day.

issues.claim: the button ending the refusal path was labelled Accept cookies, which misled users about what they were doing
issues.source_says: Paragraph 113 and 114: to refuse, the user had to click 'Gerer les parametres de donnees', scroll the second window and then click 'Accepter les cookies'; the formation restreinte holds it 'particulierement contre-intuitif de devoir cliquer sur un bouton intitule Accepter les cookies' to refuse. Paragraph 109 of the same published text calls that final button 'Tout accepter', an internal inconsistency in the anonymised version.

issues.claim: the CNIL has since closed the injunction
issues.source_says: Not addressed in this deliberation.

note: Dispositif confirms 60 million euros on FACEBOOK IRELAND LIMITED, article 82, injunction of equivalent simplicity, 100,000 euros per day after three months.

issues.claim: An injunction required a refusal mechanism as simple as acceptance within three months, backed by 60,000 euros per day of delay.
issues.source_says: Dispositif: the injunction is 'de recueillir le consentement des utilisateurs lors de leur arrivee sur le site web bing.com avant toute operation de lecture et ecriture d'informations sur le terminal des utilisateurs residant en France ayant pour finalite la lutte contre la fraude publicitaire', with an astreinte of 60 000 euros per day after three months. The injunction does not cover the refusal mechanism, which the company had already changed on 29 March 2022 (paragraph 13).

issues.claim: offered no first-layer button to refuse cookies, while acceptance took one click
issues.source_says: Paragraphs 65 and 70 to 73: the banner had an immediate accept button but no equivalent one-click refusal; refusing took at least two further actions via 'Plus d'options' and 'Enregistrer les parametres'.

proposed_takeaway: The CNIL fined Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited 60 million euros because bing.com wrote an advertising cookie to the terminal before any consent and offered no first-layer button to refuse cookies, while acceptance took one click, in breach of article 82. An injunction required consent to be collected on arrival at bing.com before any write used for advertising fraud detection, within three months, backed by 60,000 euros per day of delay. The case confirms that a cookie used for both fraud detection and advertising still needs consent. Search engines and other high-traffic services operating in France are treated as within the CNIL's direct reach.
note: Fine, article and astreinte all correct; the injunction was about consent before the MUID write, not about the refusal path.

Secondary source confirms both entities, 5 million euros, May 2020 to June 2022, one-click accept versus several clicks to refuse, inadequate purpose information in banner and consent tool, article 82, and the aggravating factors including minors and prior CNIL communications.

issues.source_says: Article 6 is the legal basis finding; articles 12 and 13 concern the exercise of rights and information given to data subjects, which are separate breaches, not part of the legal basis failure.

Customer-matching uploads to ad platforms need their own legal basis, separate from the cookie banner.
note: Amount, 30 December 2025 date, February 2018 start, eleven cookies, post-refusal reading and 10.5 million people all confirmed; only the article grouping needed fixing.

Provvedimento n. 231 of 10 June 2021 confirmed: Gazzetta Ufficiale n. 163 of 9 July 2021, six months to comply, scroll alone insufficient, cookie walls unlawful absent an equivalent alternative, X top right with graphic parity leaving defaults untouched, re-presentation after at least six months or a material change, and analytics exempt only with at least the fourth IP octet masked and no cross-site combination, under article 122 of the Codice.

issues.source_says: The post cites only § 19 Abs. 1 EinwV, and attributes both duties to it: providers must 'dafuer Sorge tragen, dass die Einstellungen der Nutzer*innen beruecksichtigt werden' and must tell users without stored settings 'welchen Dienst der Anbieter nutzt'. § 18 EinwV is not mentioned anywhere on the page.

proposed_takeaway: On 17 October 2025 the Federal Commissioner (BfDI) recognised the first service under the Einwilligungsverwaltungsverordnung, the PIMS Consenter from Law & Innovation Technology GmbH, and entered it in the public register required by section 13 EinwV. Recognition makes the section 19 EinwV duties concrete for any German digital service that chooses to integrate the service: stored end-user settings must be honoured, and users without stored settings must be told which service the provider uses and that settings can be made there. Consent platforms operating in Germany should decide whether to interoperate with recognised services and document that decision.
note: Date, BfDI, Consenter, Law & Innovation Technology GmbH and the section 13 register all confirmed; only the section 18 reference is unsupported.

issues.claim: so the consent is invalid under section 25 TTDSG and the GDPR

issues.source_says: The article says a Verbraucherverband sued a weather portal, but does not name the UWG or any other statutory basis for the claim.

proposed_takeaway: The OLG Koeln held that a banner offering Accept, Settings and an X labelled Accept and close in the corner on the first layer, and only Save or Accept all on the second, gave users no rejection option equivalent to the consent option on either layer, and that pairing the X with Accept and close was misleading and intransparent, so the consent is invalid under section 25 TTDSG. The claim was brought by a consumer association against a weather portal; the judgment (6 U 80/23, 19 January 2024) is not final. Site operators in Germany face civil injunctions from competitors and associations, not only regulators, for asymmetric banners; give both options the same layer and weight.
note: Case number, date and the X finding match; the first layer versus second layer framing is the substantive error.

proposed_takeaway: The AP announced that, since it began structural checks in April 2025, it had warned more than 200 websites about their cookie banners, that about three quarters had already adjusted them, and that it was now taking enforcement steps against those that had not. Its position is that tracking cookies may be placed only with voluntary consent given on the basis of clear and correct information, and that the simplest way to respect users' choice is not to use tracking software at all, so no banner is needed. Organisations serving Dutch users should treat an AP warning as the last step before a formal investigation.
note: Date 11 November 2025, the three quarters figure and the enforcement step all confirmed; the start date of the structural checks is wrong.

issues.source_says: The news page confirms the guidelines 'indeholder fire kriterier' and gives the assessment points from the Gul og Gratis decision (a payment alternative exists, pricing is not unreasonably high, the paid service is largely equivalent, statistical processing must be shown necessary or separately consented), but the four criteria themselves sit on a separate guidance page that returned 404 on both path variants, so their exact wording could not be read.

issues.source_says: The news page says nothing about replacing or withdrawing earlier guidance; it only announces that the two authorities have published a joint guidance covering 'de vaesentligste regler i cookiebekendtgoerelsen og databeskyttelsesforordningen'.

issues.claim: in particular the treatment of statistics cookies
issues.source_says: Statistics cookies are not singled out on the news page.

The guidance goes through the main rules of each regime, gives practical advice and examples, and flags the typical pitfalls. Danish-facing sites should re-check banners against it, in particular the treatment of statistics cookies.

issues.claim: raises the penalty surcharge to up to 3 percent of total related sales
issues.source_says: Article 64-2(1): a penalty surcharge 'within the scope not exceeding 3/100 of the total sales', with a cap of two billion won where there are no sales or sales cannot be calculated. Article 64-2(2): the surcharge is calculated 'based on the gross sales net of the sales unrelated to the violation'. The phrase 'related sales' does not appear anywhere in the Act; moving the base from related sales to total sales was the point of the 2023 amendment.

issues.claim: automatic collection devices such as cookies

proposed_takeaway: The amended Act, in force from 15 September 2023, unifies the rules for online service providers and other controllers, requires consent to collect personal information unless another basis applies, requires separate consent for marketing and third-party provision, requires the privacy policy to describe the installation, operation and refusal of automatic collection devices such as cookies, adds a right to refuse automated decisions, and raises the penalty surcharge under Article 64-2 to up to 3 percent of total sales, calculated net of sales unrelated to the violation. It binds domestic and foreign operators processing Korean residents' data. Provide granular opt-in consent for behavioural advertising cookies, keep the cookie section of the privacy policy current, and expect PIPC audits of consent screens.
note: PIPC's index row 'Personal Information Protection Act [Enforcement Date September 15, 2023]' leads to the official English text (Act No. 19234, 14 March 2023); Chapter VI is marked 'Deleted', confirming unification, and Articles 22, 30(1)7, 31-2 and 37-2 confirm the rest.

proposed_takeaway: The PDPL, amended by Royal Decree M/148 of 5/9/1444 AH (March 2023) and in force 720 days after publication under Article 43, requires a lawful basis for processing, consent that can be withdrawn at any time (Article 5), and a privacy policy made available before collection (Article 12), and its Implementing Regulations allow direct marketing only with the data subject's consent, with the sender identified and a way to stop the messages that is as easy as giving consent (Article 29). Fines reach SAR 5 million and may be doubled for a repeat violation (Article 36), with the competent authority supervising, and parties outside the Kingdom processing residents' data are bound (Article 2). Treat advertising cookies as consent-based and include a marketing opt-out in the banner's second layer.

proposed_takeaway: Amendment 13, in force from 14 August 2025, modernises the 1981 law by widening the definitions of personal and sensitive data, requiring that a request for information state whether provision is mandatory, the purposes, recipients and rights, giving the Privacy Protection Authority powers to audit, order and impose administrative fines, and extending duties to outsourced holders processing data for a controller. Direct marketing databases remain subject to the database registration and opt-out rules. Practitioners should present cookie notices with the statutory disclosure items and maintain an easy opt-out from direct marketing profiles built from tracking data.
note: Entry URL is the Authority's department landing page and returns only meta tags; verified against the Authority's own Amendment 13 guide, which confirms the date, the definitions, the notice items, the enforcement powers and the direct marketing registration and deletion rules.

issues.claim: lets any person opt out of processing for advertising at any time and without cost (Article 27)
issues.source_says: Article 27 paragraph 3: 'El titular podrá en cualquier momento solicitar el retiro o bloqueo de su nombre de los bancos de datos a los que se refiere el presente artículo.' (at any time, no mention of cost). The free-of-charge wording sits in paragraph 2 and attaches to the right of access: 'el titular de los datos podrá ejercer el derecho de acceso sin cargo alguno.'

issues.claim: The Agency of Access to Public Information enforces it
issues.source_says: Article 29 creates an 'órgano de control' as a decentralised body within the Ministry of Justice and Human Rights and does not name the Agency; Article 31 sets fines of 1,000 to 100,000 pesos.

proposed_takeaway: Law 25.326 requires free, express and informed consent, in writing or by an equivalent means, before personal data is processed unless an exception applies (Article 5), requires notice of purpose and recipients (Article 6), and lets any person ask at any time for the removal or blocking of their name from advertising databases, with access to those records free of charge (Article 27). The Agency of Access to Public Information enforces it with fines that remain low under the current scale; a replacement bill with turnover-based fines has been pending since 2023. It binds controllers in Argentina and those using means there. Present advertising cookies as opt-in and provide a no-cost objection route for marketing profiles.
note: Articles 5, 6 and 27 confirmed word for word; only the attachment of 'without cost' to the opt-out rather than to access is off.

issues.claim: has sanctioned operators for collecting data through websites without valid authorisation
issues.source_says: Law 1581 gives the Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio the power to investigate and sanction (articles 19, 21 and 23) but records no enforcement history; the statute does not address specific website cases.

note: Article 3(a) defines authorisation as 'Consentimiento previo, expreso e informado del Titular'; article 23(a) sets fines up to 2,000 monthly minimum wages; article 2 extends the law to controllers abroad by international norms and treaties; Decree 1377 article 7 allows authorisation by 'conductas inequivocas' and article 8 puts the proof on the controller.

issues.claim: require controllers to use the least intrusive means of profiling
issues.source_says: The phrase 'least intrusive' does not appear anywhere in the Data Protection (General) Regulations 2021. Part on commercial use runs regulation 14 (meaning of commercial purposes), regulation 15 (use of personal data for commercial purposes, consent or an unexercised opt out) and regulation 16 (features of an opt out message: visible, clear, minimal time and effort, direct channel, free of charge, accessible to persons with a disability).

issues.claim: penalties of up to KES 5 million or 1 percent of annual turnover
issues.source_says: Section 63 caps the administrative fine at five million shillings or, in the case of an undertaking, one per centum of its annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is lower.

issues.claim: has issued determinations against operators for unsolicited marketing
issues.source_says: Neither the Act nor the General Regulations records any determination; ODPC determinations are separate published decisions.

proposed_takeaway: The Act, in force from 25 November 2019, requires a lawful basis including consent that is express, unequivocal, free, specific and informed, and the General Regulations of 2021 permit direct marketing only with consent or to existing customers who have not opted out, and require the opt out route to be visible, easy and free of charge. The Office of the Data Protection Commissioner enforces with penalties of up to KES 5 million or 1 percent of annual turnover, whichever is lower, and has issued determinations against operators for unsolicited marketing. It binds controllers in Kenya and those processing Kenyan residents' data. Treat advertising cookies as consent-based and honour marketing opt-outs across channels.
note: Act checked at kentrade copy: assent 8 November 2019, commencement 25 November 2019, s2 consent definition word for word as quoted, s4 extraterritorial scope, s63 fine cap. Regulations checked at the ODPC copy.

issues.claim: The Commission's General Application and Implementation Directive of 2025 adds detailed rules on consent design, cookie notices and privacy policies
issues.source_says: Confirmed in the GAID: Article 17 on reliance on consent (17(6) record of consent, 17(7) withdrawal as easy as giving), Article 19 on cookies (19(4) banner conspicuous and obvious, 19(6) necessary cookies distinguished from those needing a yes or no selection, 19(7)(a) banner appears first without scrolling), Articles 7(l) and 27 on privacy notices, Article 18(1)(a) direct marketing on consent, Article 8 on controllers of major importance.

issues.claim: penalties of up to the greater of NGN 10 million and 2 per cent of annual gross revenue for controllers of major importance (NGN 2 million or 2 per cent for others)
issues.source_says: The GAID carries no NGN penalty figures or percentages of annual gross revenue; those sit in the Act, which could not be reached.

The Act itself was not reached: cert.gov.ng returns 403 behind Cloudflare, the placng.org copy is a scan with no machine-readable text, NDPC publishes no Act PDF, and the ICNL copy exists but Chrome's viewer yields no text while WebFetch refuses the URL.

issues.source_says: The law provides for an authority set up by presidential regulation but cannot state what had or had not happened by October 2024.

note: Art 22(1) written or recorded consent, Art 22(4) clearly distinguishable and plain language, Art 9 withdrawal, Art 10 objection to automated decisions and profiling, Art 57(3) fine up to 2 percent of annual revenue, Art 74 two-year transition, enacted 17 October 2022.

issues.claim: requires controllers to give users a way to refuse tracking and personalised advertising
issues.source_says: The page places this duty on a specific sector, not on controllers generally: under its social network and online service section, "Organizations must provide a Do-not-track option" and "Organizations must provide opt-outs for cookies and tracking."

issues.claim: fines of up to 5 percent of the previous year's revenue for unlawful cross-border transfers and up to ten times the revenue gained from unlawful sale of personal data
issues.source_says: Both figures carry a floor the takeaway omits: "fines can reach up to 5% of organizations' previous year's revenue or VND 3 billion (around EUR 100.000), whichever is higher" and "the maximum fine is either ten times the revenue gained from the violation or VND 3 billion, whichever is higher".

issues.claim: Decree 13/2023/ND-CP (in force from 1 July 2023)
issues.source_says: The page gives only the year: the PDPD, "also called Decree No. 13/2023/ND-CP, that came into effect in 2023". It does not state 1 July 2023.

proposed_takeaway: The Law, passed on 26 June 2025 and in force from 1 January 2026, carries forward the consent standard of Decree 13/2023/ND-CP (in force from 1 July 2023): consent must be voluntary, specific, informed and given per purpose, and silence is not consent. It adds fines of up to 5 percent of the previous year's revenue for unlawful cross-border transfers and up to ten times the revenue gained from unlawful sale of personal data, in each case the higher of that figure and VND 3 billion, and requires social network and online service providers to offer a do-not-track option and opt-outs for cookies and tracking. It binds domestic and foreign controllers processing Vietnamese residents' data. Present cookie consent per purpose and provide a working tracking opt-out.
note: Declared secondary; the explainer confirms the law number, both dates, the consent tests and extraterritorial scope, but scopes the tracking opt-out to social network and online services and attaches a VND 3 billion floor to both fines.

Brave announced Global Privacy Control on 7 October 2020, first in the Nightly desktop channel and the Android beta, and the signal is on by default in every version that implements it, described as a way for users to assert legal privacy rights, with an option to turn it off. These are browser defaults, not law. A business that receives Sec-GPC: 1 from a Brave visitor in a state that recognises the signal must treat it as an opt-out of sale, sharing and targeted advertising.

It also sets out the ICO's position on consent or pay models and further engagement with consent management platforms. Audit banners so that non-essential advertising cookies are not set before a choice is made and rejecting is as easy as accepting.

It applies to every organisation designing online interfaces for UK consumers; the ICO warns it will act against businesses that deliberately and persistently design unfairly, and the CMA warns that businesses standing in the way risk action from either regulator. Use the paper as the UK benchmark for banner and preference-centre design.

issues.claim: tracking needs consent only where it reaches sensitive data or high-risk profiling
issues.source_says: The Act contains no rule on tracking technologies. Art. 6 para. 7 lists the cases needing express consent (sensitive personal data, high-risk profiling by a private person, profiling by a federal body); it does not address tracking as such.

note: Art. 6(6) voluntary and informed, Art. 6(7) express consent, Art. 5(g) high-risk profiling, Art. 19(4) countries of disclosure abroad and Art. 60 CHF 250,000 fine on private persons all check out.

issues.claim: or where the processing is necessary for the service
issues.source_says: Art. 45c let. a permits processing 'for telecommunications services and charging purposes' ('fuer Fernmeldedienste und Verrechnungszwecke'). The statute has no necessity test and the takeaway drops the charging limb.

issues.claim: which covers setting and reading cookies and similar identifiers
issues.source_says: Art. 45c speaks only of 'processing of data on external equipment by means of transmission using telecommunications techniques'. Cookies are not named.

issues.claim: It binds every operator of a website or app reaching users in Switzerland; the FDPIC applies it cumulatively with the FADP, reads the refusal requirement as a mandatory opt-out control

proposed_takeaway: Article 45c permits the processing of data on external equipment by means of transmission using telecommunications techniques, which covers setting and reading cookies and similar identifiers, only where users are informed about the processing and its purpose and are informed that they may refuse it, or where the processing is for telecommunications services and charging purposes. It binds every operator of a website or app reaching users in Switzerland; the FDPIC applies it cumulatively with the FADP, reads the refusal requirement as a mandatory opt-out control, and cites a fine of up to CHF 5,000 under Article 53 TCA. Provide the notice and a refusal control before any non-necessary cookie is set.
